meta.title: Revenue Casebook
meta.huntQuestion: Which Ind AS 115 paragraph decides this?
meta.tagline: Find the step. *Then* apply the paragraph.
meta.intro: {cases} Ind AS 115 questions: every SM illustration, TYK and practice question, and every RTP, MTP and past-paper question from May 2022 to Nov 2026.

P.label: Ind AS 115 · core
P.title: Core principle, definitions and the five-step model
P.law:
An entity shall recognise revenue to depict the transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled in exchange. Five steps: (1) identify the contract; (2) identify the performance obligations; (3) determine the transaction price; (4) allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations; (5) recognise revenue when (or as) each performance obligation is satisfied.

As a practical expedient the Standard may be applied to a portfolio of contracts (or performance obligations) with similar characteristics if the effect would not differ materially from applying it contract by contract.
notes: Contract: an agreement between two or more parties that creates enforceable rights and obligations.

Contract asset: right to consideration for goods/services already transferred when that right is conditioned on something other than the passage of time (e.g. the entity's future performance). Contract liability: obligation to transfer goods/services for which consideration has been received (or is due).

Performance obligation: a promise to transfer (a) a distinct good or service (or bundle), or (b) a series of distinct goods or services that are substantially the same and have the same pattern of transfer.
Revenue = income arising in the course of ordinary activities. Transaction price excludes amounts collected on behalf of third parties.
Stand-alone selling price: the price at which the entity would sell the good or service separately to a customer.
Ind AS 115 supersedes Ind AS 11 and Ind AS 18. Judgement is applied consistently to contracts with similar characteristics, including implied terms.
Portfolio approach in use: SM Illustration 34 (1,000 sales with a 30-day return right treated as one portfolio).
P.mem: C-P-T-A-S: Contract → Performance obligations → Transaction price → Allocate → Satisfy.

P.label: Ind AS 115.5–8
P.title: Scope: what is inside and what is excluded
P.law:
Apply to all contracts with customers except: (a) leases (Ind AS 116); (b) insurance contracts (Ind AS 117), though fixed-fee service-type insurance contracts may be brought in; (c) financial instruments and other rights or obligations within Ind AS 109, 110, 111, 27 and 28; (d) non-monetary exchanges between entities in the same line of business to facilitate sales to customers or potential customers (e.g. two oil companies swapping oil to meet demand in different locations).

A customer is a party that has contracted to obtain goods or services that are an output of the entity's ordinary activities in exchange for consideration.
notes: A counterparty that shares the risks and benefits of an activity (a collaboration, e.g. jointly developing an asset) is not a customer.

Partly in scope: if the other Ind AS says how to separate/measure a portion, apply it first and exclude that amount from the transaction price; otherwise use Ind AS 115 (relative stand-alone selling prices) to separate.
Ind AS 115 also governs incremental costs of obtaining and costs of fulfilling a contract not covered by another Standard.
Barter of dissimilar goods/services (print vs TV advertising; talk time vs power) is in scope: measure the non-cash consideration at fair value (SM TYK 1 and 2).
Interest and dividends are outside Ind AS 115 (financial instruments standards).
P.mem: Exclusions LIFE: Leases, Insurance, Financial instruments, Exchanges in the same line of business.

P.label: Ind AS 115 · C3
P.title: Transition: full retrospective or modified retrospective
P.law: On first application an entity uses either (a) the full retrospective approach: restate each prior period presented under Ind AS 8 (subject to practical expedients), so comparatives look as if Ind AS 115 always applied; or (b) the modified retrospective approach: no restatement of prior periods; the cumulative effect of initial application is recognised in opening retained earnings of the year of first application.
notes: The SM states Ind AS 115 is effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 April 20X2 (SM dates are stylised; Ind AS 115 was notified by MCA in March 2018).
Choice matters for comparatives: full retrospective restates them; modified retrospective leaves them on the old basis.

P.label: Ind AS 115 vs AS 7/9
P.title: Significant differences between Ind AS 115 and AS 7 / AS 9
P.law: Ind AS 115 gives a single control-based five-step framework with a core principle; AS 9 uses transfer of significant risks and rewards and AS 7 uses stage of completion for construction contracts. Ind AS 115 adds guidance AS 7/9 lack: multiple-element arrangements, combining contracts, variable and contingent consideration, time value of money (significant financing), capitalisation of contract costs, service concession arrangements and detailed disclosures.
notes: Measurement: Ind AS 115 uses the transaction price (consideration expected to be entitled, excluding third-party collections); AS 9 uses gross inflow of cash, receivables or other consideration.
Coverage: AS 7 = construction contracts only; AS 9 = sale of goods, services, interest, royalties and dividends; Ind AS 115 excludes interest and dividends.
Financing: AS 9 recognises the full ₹1,21,000 as revenue; Ind AS 115 splits ₹1,00,000 revenue and ₹21,000 interest (SM Illustration 38).
Warranties: AS 9 makes a general provision (e.g. 5% of revenue); Ind AS 115 separates assurance-type (Ind AS 37) and service-type (contract liability) (SM Illustration 35).
Contract acquisition cost: AS 9 expenses a ₹1 crore commission at once; Ind AS 115 capitalises and amortises it (SM Example 8).

P.label: Ind AS 115.9–16
P.title: Step 1: the five criteria for a contract, and consideration received before they are met
P.law:
Account for a contract only when all are met: (a) the parties have approved it (in writing, orally or by customary business practice) and are committed to perform; (b) each party's rights can be identified; (c) the payment terms can be identified; (d) the contract has commercial substance; (e) it is probable the entity will collect the consideration to which it will be entitled (considering only the customer's ability and intention to pay when due).

If the criteria are not met, consideration received is recognised as revenue only when (a) the entity has no remaining obligations and all, or substantially all, consideration is received and non-refundable, or (b) the contract is terminated and the consideration is non-refundable. Until then it is a liability measured at the consideration received (para 15–16).
notes: Step 1 is a gateway: Steps 2–5 are not applied until the criteria are met; once met, reassess only on a significant change in facts (e.g. the customer's ability to pay deteriorates sharply). Reassessment is prospective: receivables and revenue already recognised are not reversed.
'Probable' means more likely than not. Credit risk decides whether a contract exists; it does not change measurement or presentation of revenue.
Collectability is tested on the amount the entity expects to be entitled to, which may be lower than the contract price if a price concession is expected (SM TYK 5: ₹1.75 million, not ₹2 million).
Payment terms need not be fixed: an enforceable right to payment plus enough information to estimate the price is sufficient.
Commercial substance blocks round-tripping goods to inflate revenue.
SM TYK 4: non-recourse finance to a customer with no other income → collection not probable → the ₹1,00,000 deposit is a deposit liability.
P.mem: A-R-P-C-C: Approved, Rights, Payment terms, Commercial substance, Collectable.

P.label: Ind AS 115.11–12
P.title: Contract term and termination rights
P.law: Apply the Standard to the duration in which the parties have present enforceable rights and obligations. A contract does not exist if each party has the unilateral enforceable right to terminate a wholly unperformed contract without compensating the other (wholly unperformed = nothing transferred and nothing receivable).
notes: If only the customer can cancel without penalty, the accounting term may be shorter than the stated term (gym: 12 months stated, cancellable without penalty after 3 → term is 3 months, SM Illustration 2).
No termination penalty after 10 units → contract for 10 units plus an option for 90 (SM Illustration 3).

A substantive termination penalty payable by the customer is evidence of enforceable rights for the whole period it covers (four-year contract with a declining substantive penalty = four-year contract), unless past experience with that customer class suggests otherwise.

P.label: Ind AS 115.17
P.title: Combining contracts
P.law: Combine two or more contracts entered into at or near the same time with the same customer (or its related parties) if any one is met: (a) negotiated as a package with a single commercial objective; (b) the consideration in one depends on the price or performance of the other; or (c) the goods or services promised are a single performance obligation.
notes: Assessed at contract inception; there is no bright line for 'near the same time' — judgement.
Separate commercial objectives → not combined (fighter planes and spare parts, SM Illustration 4).
Licence plus customisation three days later that the customer cannot use without → combined (SM Illustration 5).
Two government entities controlled by the same government, deep discount only if both buy → combined (related parties, single package, dependent consideration; SM Illustration 6).
P.mem: Combine if same customer + same time + one of: Package, Price-dependent, Performance obligation is single.

P.label: Ind AS 115.18–21
P.title: Contract modifications
P.law: A modification is a change in scope or price (or both) approved by the parties and enforceable. It is a separate contract if (1) scope increases by distinct goods or services and (2) price increases by their stand-alone selling price (adjusted for, e.g., lower selling costs for a repeat customer). Otherwise: (a) remaining goods/services distinct → treat as termination of the old contract and creation of a new one (prospective); (b) remaining goods/services not distinct (part of a partly satisfied single performance obligation) → cumulative catch-up adjustment to revenue at the modification date; (c) mix of both → combine the two methods.
notes: Common forms: partial termination, extension of term, adding goods/services, reducing price without changing scope.
Separate contract: 30 extra products at ₹950 = their stand-alone price → new contract; original 120 at ₹1,000 unaffected (SM Illustration 7).
Prospective: maintenance reduced from ₹55,000 to ₹45,000 a month after six months → remaining consideration ₹2,70,000 allocated to the remaining services (SM Illustration 8).
Cumulative catch-up: 200 hours × ₹150 plus 50 hours × ₹100 → ₹35,000 ÷ 250 = ₹140 an hour; 100 hours done → revenue to date ₹14,000 vs ₹15,000 booked → reduce revenue by ₹1,000 (SM Illustration 9).
A modification can make a separate contract out of an addition to a series if priced at stand-alone selling price.
Discretionary credits that are a change in price (not variable consideration) are accounted for as a modification over the remaining term (SM Illustration 58).
P.mem: Distinct + SSP → separate contract. Distinct only → fresh start. Not distinct → catch-up.

P.label: Ind AS 115.22–30
P.title: Step 2: promises and distinct goods or services
P.law:
At inception assess the goods or services promised and identify each promise to transfer a distinct good or service (or bundle) as a performance obligation. A good or service is distinct if both: (a) capable of being distinct — the customer can benefit from it on its own or with other readily available resources; and (b) distinct in the context of the contract — the promise is separately identifiable from other promises.

Not separately identifiable if: (i) the entity provides a significant integration service (inputs to a combined output); (ii) one item significantly modifies or customises another; or (iii) the items are highly interdependent or highly interrelated (a two-way dependency).
notes: Promises can be implicit: customary business practices, published policies or specific statements that create a valid expectation (free telephone support to reseller's customers, SM Illustration 20; carmaker's two-year free maintenance in advertisements, SM Illustration 21).
Set-up/administrative activities that transfer nothing to the customer are not performance obligations (activation of a data connection, SM Illustration 28).
Benefit = use, consume, sell for more than scrap value, or hold to generate economic benefits. Regularly selling an item separately indicates it is capable of being distinct.

Single performance obligation: water purification plant and power plant with integration (SM Illustrations 10, 12); design-and-build shopping centre (Illustration 14); licence + significant customisation (Illustration 16); anti-virus licence + critical updates (Illustration 18).

Separate performance obligations: broadband, voice, modem (Illustration 11); licence, installation, updates, support (Illustration 15: four); modem, router, internet (Illustration 17: three); print copy and online access (Illustration 19: two).
If items are not distinct, keep combining them until a distinct bundle results; the whole contract may be one performance obligation. The same items can be treated differently in different contracts.
P.mem: Distinct = Capable (can benefit) AND Separately identifiable (no Integration, no Modification, no Interdependence) — 'C and S, not I-M-I'.

P.label: Ind AS 115.22(b), 23
P.title: Series of distinct goods or services and long-term arrangements
P.law: A series of distinct goods or services that are substantially the same and have the same pattern of transfer is a single performance obligation when (a) each distinct item would be a performance obligation satisfied over time, and (b) the same method would measure progress for each. Applying the series requirement is not optional.
notes: Examples: cleaning, transaction processing, delivering electricity, hotel management (day-to-day activities vary but each time increment of 'hotel management' is substantially the same, SM Illustration 13).
Stand-ready processing contract: each day of access (or each transaction) can be the distinct item (SM Example 2).

Long-term arrangements: a contract renewable or cancellable by either party at discrete points may be accounted for period by period; with fixed consideration the result is usually the same (cable TV for 3 years = one performance obligation satisfied over time, SM Illustration 24).
Asset management services with quarterly fees are a series (SM Illustration 33); weekly services for shares (Illustration 48).

P.label: Ind AS 115.B39–B43
P.title: Customer options: material rights, loyalty points and renewal options
P.law:
An option to acquire additional goods or services is a separate performance obligation only if it gives a material right — a discount the customer would not receive without entering into the contract (e.g. beyond the range typically given to that class of customer). The customer in effect pays in advance; revenue is recognised when the future goods/services transfer or the option expires. If the option price equals stand-alone selling price it is a marketing offer, accounted for only when exercised.

If not directly observable, estimate the option's stand-alone selling price from the discount on exercise, adjusted for (a) any discount available without the option and (b) the likelihood of exercise.
notes: Discount voucher: 40% voucher but 10% available to all → only the incremental 30% is a material right; SSP = ₹500 × 30% × 80% = ₹120; allocate ₹1,000 as ₹890 product / ₹110 voucher (SM Illustration 23).

Renewal at a discount: 100 members at ₹7,500, renewals at ₹6,000, 50% attrition → 175 expected memberships, ₹12,00,000 total → ₹6,857 per membership; ₹643 per first-year member is a contract liability (SM Illustration 22).

Loyalty points that are a material right: allocate part of the sale price to the points on relative stand-alone selling prices (considering expected redemption) and recognise it as points are redeemed or lapse (SM Practice Questions 5 and 9).
Points redeemable with another party: consider whether the entity is a principal or agent for the points.
P.mem: Material right = a discount you get only because you signed. Price it: discount × chance of use, net of what everyone gets anyway.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B77–B78
P.title: Consignment arrangements
P.law: Indicators of consignment: (a) the entity controls the product until a specified event (sale to the dealer's customer) or period expires; (b) the entity can require return or transfer to a third party (another dealer); (c) the dealer has no unconditional obligation to pay (though a deposit may be required). Revenue is not recognised on delivery to the consignee; it is recognised when control transfers (sale to the end customer or expiry of the agreed period).
notes: Consignment differs from a sale with a right of return: in a right-of-return sale the customer has control and decides whether to return.
60-day consignment of 1,000 dresses, retailer pays ₹20 per dress only when sold; manufacturer can require return or transfer → revenue as dresses are sold to end customers (SM Illustration 25).
An unconditional right of return can make a 'sale' a consignment in substance.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B34–B38
P.title: Principal versus agent
P.law:
When another party is involved, determine whether the entity's promise is to provide the specified good or service itself (principal → revenue at the gross amount) or to arrange for another party to provide it (agent → revenue at the net fee or commission). The test is whether the entity controls the specified good or service before transfer.

Indicators of principal: (a) primarily responsible for fulfilling the contract (acceptability); (b) inventory risk before transfer or after (e.g. right of return); (c) discretion in establishing prices.
notes: Momentary legal title just before transfer does not by itself make an entity a principal.
Travel entity buying airline tickets in advance, bearing unsold-ticket risk and setting prices → principal for the ticket (right to fly), gross revenue (SM Illustration 26).

Advertiser D using F Ltd. to place ads: D directs F, works with customers and is responsible for meeting needs → principal even without inventory risk or pricing discretion (SM Illustration 27). The indicators support, not replace, the control assessment.

Loyalty points redeemable with another party: if the entity is an agent for the points, its obligation may be satisfied when the points are transferred; if the points give future goods from the entity itself, it is not an agent.
If the customer later chooses goods from a third party and the entity acted as agent, it recognises only its fee or commission.
P.mem: Principal = R-I-P: Responsible, Inventory risk, Pricing discretion — but control decides.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B48–B51
P.title: Non-refundable upfront fees
P.law: Assess whether the fee relates to transfer of a promised good or service. If the related activity at or near inception does not transfer a good or service (e.g. joining, activation or set-up fees), the fee is an advance payment for future goods or services and is recognised as revenue when those are provided (possibly over future contract periods, including expected renewals where the fee gives a material right).
notes: If the fee does relate to a good or service, evaluate whether that is a separate performance obligation.
Set-up activities that are not performance obligations are ignored when measuring progress (their costs do not depict transfer).
Data-connection activation fee: activation is not a service to the customer → not a separate performance obligation; the obligation is to provide data services (SM Illustration 28).
Examples in the SM: health-club joining fees, telecom activation fees, set-up fees, initial fees in supply contracts.

P.label: Ind AS 115.47–49
P.title: Step 3: what the transaction price is
P.law: The transaction price is the amount of consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled for transferring the promised goods or services, excluding amounts collected on behalf of third parties (e.g. some sales taxes). It may be fixed, variable or both. Assume the goods/services transfer as promised and the contract will not be cancelled, renewed or modified. Consider: variable consideration and the constraint, a significant financing component, non-cash consideration and consideration payable to a customer.
notes: Revenue recognised = transaction price allocated to a satisfied performance obligation, excluding constrained variable consideration.
The customer's credit risk does not reduce the transaction price (it is a collectability or Ind AS 109 matter).
P.mem: Four things move the price: Variable, Financing, Non-cash, Payable to customer (V-F-N-P).

P.label: Ind AS 115.50–54
P.title: Variable consideration and how to estimate it
P.law: Consideration is variable because of discounts, rebates, refunds, credits, price concessions, incentives, performance bonuses, penalties, or entitlement contingent on a future event (e.g. a right of return or a milestone bonus). It is also variable if the customer has a valid expectation of a concession from customary practice or the entity intends one. Estimate it by the method that better predicts the amount: (a) expected value (sum of probability-weighted amounts; suits many similar contracts); or (b) most likely amount (suits two possible outcomes). Apply one method consistently for an uncertainty; different uncertainties in one contract may use different methods.
notes: Penalties: account per substance. If inherent in the price (₹1,00,000 if delivered within 30 days, else ₹95,000) the ₹5,000 is variable consideration; otherwise the price is fixed at ₹95,000 (SM Example 3).

Early-completion bonus with a range → expected value: 15% × ₹25 crore × 25% + 10% × 40% + 5% × 15% = ₹2.125 crore; quality bonus (two outcomes) → most likely ₹2 crore; transaction price ₹29.125 crore (SM Illustration 30).
Daily penalty/incentive → expected value; ₹15 lakh rating bonus → most likely amount (SM Illustration 29).
Price protection: expected reimbursement ₹50 → transaction price ₹950 (SM Practice Question 1); expected-value TV price protection (PQ 2); two-outcome completion bonus → most likely ₹1,30,000 (PQ 3).
Retrospective volume tiers: estimate the year's volume (2.8 million → ₹90 a container) and recognise a liability for cash above it (SM TYK 6). Rebate coupons: ₹50 − 25% × ₹10 = ₹47.50 (TYK 7).
Then apply the constraint.
P.mem: Many outcomes → Expected value. Two outcomes → Most likely.

P.label: Ind AS 115.56–59
P.title: Constraint on variable consideration and reassessment
P.law:
Include variable consideration only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal in cumulative revenue recognised will not occur when the uncertainty is resolved — considering both likelihood and magnitude. Factors increasing reversal risk: (a) amount highly susceptible to factors outside the entity's influence (market volatility, third parties' judgement, weather, obsolescence); (b) uncertainty not resolved for a long time; (c) limited or non-predictive experience; (d) a practice of broad price concessions or changing payment terms; (e) a large number and broad range of possible amounts.

At each reporting date update the estimate (and the constraint) and account for changes under paras 87–90.
notes: Asset-management fees based on market value and a 5-year performance fee → constrained at inception; each quarter's management fee is included once known (₹2 crore on ₹100 crore AUM); the incentive fee stays constrained (SM Illustration 33).
Volume discount not expected in Q1 → ₹10,000 at ₹1,000; after the customer's acquisition, Q2 revenue = 50 × ₹900 − 10 × ₹100 = ₹44,000 (SM Illustration 31).
Weight incentive: 10% included (95% confidence); revised to 25% in year 4 with a cumulative catch-up of ₹98,683 (SM Illustration 32).
Lack of experience → bonus not included at inception (SM Illustration 57).
P.mem: Include only what you would not have to give back: likelihood × size of reversal.

P.label: Ind AS 115.55, B20–B27
P.title: Refund liabilities and sale with a right of return
P.short: Right of return and refund liability
P.law: Recognise a refund liability for consideration received (or receivable) that the entity does not expect to be entitled to; update it each reporting date. For a sale with a right of return recognise: (a) revenue only for products not expected to be returned; (b) a refund liability; and (c) an asset (with a matching adjustment to cost of sales) for the right to recover products, measured at the former carrying amount less expected recovery costs (including any fall in value). Present the asset separately from the refund liability. The promise to stand ready to accept returns is not a separate performance obligation.
notes: 1,000 products at ₹50, cost ₹30, 970 expected to be kept → revenue ₹48,500, refund liability ₹1,500, asset ₹900 (SM Illustration 34).
Restocking fee: include in the transaction price at inception. 10 units at ₹100, 10% returns, 3% fee → revenue ₹903, refund liability ₹97 (SM Example 4).
Exchanges of one product for another of the same type, quality, condition and price are not returns. Defective-for-working swaps are warranties.
Refund liabilities also arise from service refunds and retrospective price reductions (volume rebates).
No experience of returns → the constraint may stop revenue until the return period ends (SM Illustration 38).
P.mem: Return = 3 entries: revenue for keepers, refund liability for returners, asset for goods coming back.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B28–B33
P.title: Warranties: assurance-type vs service-type
P.law: If the customer can purchase the warranty separately, it is a distinct service: a performance obligation to which part of the transaction price is allocated. If not, it is a performance obligation only if it gives a service in addition to assurance that the product meets agreed specifications; pure assurance-type warranties are provisions under Ind AS 37. Factors: (a) required by law (suggests assurance); (b) length of cover (longer suggests service); (c) nature of tasks (tasks needed to give assurance, e.g. return shipping of defective items, are not a service). If both types exist and cannot be separated, treat them together as one performance obligation.
notes: Laws imposing compensation for harm caused by products, and indemnities for IP-infringement claims, are not performance obligations (Ind AS 37).

Computer ₹36,000 (SSP ₹32,000 + extended warranty ₹4,000), 90-day assurance cost ₹2,000, inventory ₹14,400: Dr Cash 36,000, Dr Warranty expense 2,000 / Cr Accrued warranty 2,000, Cr Contract liability 4,000, Cr Revenue 32,000; Dr COGS / Cr Inventory 14,400 (SM Illustration 35).
Five-year battery guarantee where one year is normal: ₹1,70,000 to batteries, ₹30,000 contract liability for years 2–5, plus ₹10,000 assurance provision (100 × ₹100) (SM Illustration 36).
Contrast AS 9: a general provision only, no revenue deferral.
P.mem: Can buy it separately or covers more than defects → service-type (defer revenue). Just 'it works' → assurance (Ind AS 37 provision).

P.label: Ind AS 115.B63–B63B
P.title: Sales-based and usage-based royalties on licences of IP
P.law: Notwithstanding the constraint, revenue from a sales- or usage-based royalty for a licence of intellectual property is recognised only when (or as) the later of: (a) the subsequent sale or usage occurs; and (b) the performance obligation to which the royalty is allocated is satisfied (or partly satisfied). This applies when the royalty relates only to a licence, or a licence is the predominant item; then it applies wholly. Otherwise the general variable-consideration rules apply.
notes: Licence B paid by 3% royalty: no revenue on transfer; recognise as the customer's sales occur (SM Illustration 56 Case A).
Royalty allocated partly to an untransferred licence → contract liability for that part even though sales occurred (₹1,77,778 in SM Illustration 56 Case B).
A licence paid solely by a sales-based royalty has no significant financing component (SM Illustration 44).
P.mem: Royalty: wait for the LATER of the sale and the licence transfer.

P.label: Ind AS 115.60–65
P.title: Significant financing component
P.law: Adjust the promised consideration for the time value of money if the payment timing gives the customer or the entity a significant benefit of financing (explicit or implied). Objective: revenue at the cash selling price. Consider (a) the difference between promised consideration and cash selling price, and (b) the combined effect of the time between transfer and payment and prevailing interest rates. Use the rate of a separate financing transaction at inception (reflecting the credit of the party financed); do not update it later. Assess significance at the contract level, not portfolio. Present interest income/expense separately from revenue, only to the extent a contract asset, receivable or contract liability exists.
notes: No significant financing (para 62) if: (a) customer paid in advance and the timing of transfer is at the customer's discretion (prepaid cards); (b) a substantial amount is variable on events outside both parties' control (sales-based royalty); (c) the difference arises for reasons other than finance and is proportional (retention money protecting the customer).
Practical expedient (para 63): ignore if the gap between transfer and payment is expected to be one year or less (SM Illustration 47).
₹1,21,000 payable in 24 months, cash price ₹1,00,000 → revenue ₹1,00,000; ₹21,000 interest over two years under Ind AS 109 (SM Illustration 38).
Contract rate 10% below the customer's 14% rate → transaction price = 60 × ₹2,12,470 discounted at 14% = ₹91,31,346 (SM Illustration 39 Case B).
Advance ₹4,000 two years ahead at the entity's 6% incremental borrowing rate: Dr Cash / Cr Contract liability 4,000; interest expense ₹494; revenue ₹4,494 (SM Illustration 40).

Judgement: ₹1,40,000 (2%) not significant; ₹14,00,000 (20%) significant (SM Illustration 37). Upfront-only service fee to manage risk, advance from low-credit customer, holdback and award fee → no significant financing (Illustrations 41–46).
P.mem: Separate the sale (cash price) from the loan (interest). Under a year? Ignore.

P.label: Ind AS 115.66–69
P.title: Non-cash consideration and customer-provided goods
P.law: Measure non-cash consideration (shares, advertising, equipment) at fair value; if fair value cannot be reasonably estimated, measure it indirectly by the stand-alone selling price of the goods or services promised in exchange. Changes in fair value after inception due to the form of the consideration (e.g. share price) do not adjust the transaction price; changes for other reasons (e.g. the entity's performance) are variable consideration subject to the constraint. Goods or services contributed by the customer that the entity controls are non-cash consideration.
notes: 100 shares per week of service: measure fair value of the shares received each week; ignore later price changes (SM Illustration 48).

Bonus of 10 lakh shares at ₹100 at inception: revenue ₹350 crore + ₹10 crore = ₹360 crore if earned; number of shares earned is variable, the price per share is fixed at inception (SM Illustration 49).
TV show for ₹1,000 + 100 ad slots (fair value ₹600) → ₹1,600; if fair value unknown → ₹1,500 SSP (SM Illustration 50).
Tooling contributed by the customer worth ₹2 crore and controlled by the supplier → transaction price ₹27 crore (SM Illustration 51).

P.label: Ind AS 115.70–72
P.title: Consideration payable to a customer
P.law: Cash, credits, coupons or vouchers paid (or payable) to a customer, or to parties buying from the customer, reduce the transaction price unless paid for a distinct good or service from the customer. If for a distinct good/service, account for it as a purchase from a supplier, but any excess over fair value reduces the transaction price; if fair value cannot be estimated, the whole payment reduces the price. A reduction is recognised at the later of when the related revenue is recognised and when the entity pays or promises to pay.
notes: Slotting fees for shelf placement → reduce price (SM Example 5). Co-operative advertising at fair value from a third-party benchmark → purchase of advertising (Example 6). Price protection → reduce price.
₹1.5 crore shelving payment against a ₹15 crore commitment → reduce each sale by 10%; first month ₹1.25 crore invoiced → revenue ₹1.125 crore (SM Illustration 52).
Port-in credit ₹2,000 on a ₹800 × 24 month plan → transaction price ₹17,200, recognised over the service period (SM Illustration 53).
Variable amounts payable (e.g. rebates to end consumers) are estimated using the variable-consideration rules (SM TYK 7).
P.mem: Paying your customer? Revenue goes down — unless you bought something real at fair value.

P.label: Ind AS 115.73–80
P.title: Step 4: allocate on relative stand-alone selling prices
P.law: Allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation on a relative stand-alone selling price basis (except for discounts and variable consideration meeting the exceptions). Best evidence is the observable price when sold separately; a list or contract price may be, but is not presumed to be, the SSP. Determine SSPs at inception and do not update for later changes. If not observable, estimate maximising observable inputs: (a) adjusted market assessment; (b) expected cost plus a margin; (c) residual approach — only if the price is highly variable or uncertain (not yet established/never sold separately).
notes: A combination of methods may be used (e.g. residual for the aggregate of uncertain items, then another method to split it).
Products A (₹5,000 observable), B (₹2,500 adjusted market), C (₹7,500 cost plus margin) for ₹10,000 → allocate ₹3,300 / ₹1,700 / ₹5,000 (SM Illustration 54).
Residual check: a residual of ₹5,000 for Product Alpha whose prices range ₹15,000–₹45,000 is not faithful → use another method (SM Illustration 55 Case C).
If a modification is a termination and new contract, update SSPs at that date; if a separate contract, determine SSPs for the new contract only.
P.mem: Observable first; else Market, Cost-plus, Residual (residual only if variable or uncertain).

P.label: Ind AS 115.81–83
P.title: Allocating a discount
P.law: A discount exists if the sum of stand-alone selling prices exceeds the promised consideration. Allocate it proportionately to all performance obligations unless all are met (para 82): (a) the entity regularly sells each distinct good/service on a stand-alone basis; (b) it regularly sells a bundle of some of them at a discount; and (c) that bundle's discount is substantially the same as the contract's, giving observable evidence of where the discount belongs — then allocate it entirely to those obligations. Allocate such a discount before using the residual approach.
notes: X ₹50,000, Y ₹25,000, Z ₹45,000; Y+Z regularly sold for ₹50,000 → the whole ₹20,000 discount goes to Y and Z; split ₹17,857 / ₹32,143 if delivered at different times (SM Illustration 55 Case A).
With Product Alpha and ₹1,30,000 total, residual = ₹30,000 (within ₹15,000–₹45,000) (Case B).
Software S, Hardware H and Accessory A: apply the para 82 tests to decide whether the discount goes only to the regularly discounted bundle (SM Practice Question 7).
P.mem: Discount spreads to all — unless a regularly sold bundle proves where it belongs.

P.label: Ind AS 115.84–86
P.title: Allocating variable consideration
P.law: Allocate a variable amount (and later changes) entirely to one performance obligation, or to one distinct good/service within a series, if both: (a) the variable payment terms relate specifically to the entity's efforts to satisfy that obligation (or a specific outcome from it); and (b) allocating it entirely there is consistent with the allocation objective considering all obligations and payment terms. Otherwise use the general relative SSP allocation.
notes: Royalty ₹20,00,000 ≈ SSP of Licence B and fixed ₹16,00,000 ≈ SSP of Licence A → royalty entirely to B (SM Illustration 56 Case A).

Fixed ₹6,00,000 + royalty ₹30,00,000 would not reflect SSPs of ₹16 lakh and ₹20 lakh → allocate both fixed and royalty in the ratio 16:20; revenue ₹3,33,333 on B, ₹2,66,667 on A; first royalty ₹4,00,000 → ₹2,22,222 revenue (B) and ₹1,77,778 contract liability (A) (Case B).
An early-completion bonus may relate only to construction, not to later maintenance; a second-year inflation uplift may relate to that year of a series.

P.label: Ind AS 115.87–90
P.title: Changes in the transaction price
P.law: Allocate later changes in the transaction price on the same basis as at inception; do not reallocate for changes in stand-alone selling prices. Amounts allocated to a satisfied performance obligation are recognised as revenue (or a reduction) in the period the price changes. Continue to allocate variable amounts entirely to one obligation if the para 85 criteria still hold. A change caused by a modification follows the modification guidance; after a modification, a change attributable to variable consideration promised before it is allocated to the pre-modification obligations if the modification was a termination-and-new-contract; other changes go to the obligations unsatisfied immediately after the modification.
notes: ₹20 lakh early bonus becomes includable on 1 July: allocate it wholly to software implementation (₹1 crore → ₹1.2 crore); cumulative revenue for that obligation = 60% × ₹1.2 crore = ₹72 lakh (SM Illustration 57).
A discretionary retention credit of ₹50 in month 14 (not expected by customers) is a change in price accounted for as a modification over the remaining term (SM Illustration 58).

P.label: Ind AS 115.31–34
P.title: Step 5: transfer of control
P.law: Recognise revenue when (or as) a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring a promised good or service (an asset); an asset is transferred when (or as) the customer obtains control — the ability to direct the use of, and obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits from, the asset, including the ability to prevent others from doing so. Decide at inception whether control transfers over time; if not, at a point in time.
notes: Benefits = potential cash inflows or savings: use, enhance other assets, settle liabilities, sell/exchange, pledge, hold.
Control replaces AS 9's 'significant risks and rewards'; risks and rewards survive only as one indicator.

P.label: Ind AS 115.35–37
P.title: Performance obligations satisfied over time
P.law: Control transfers over time if any one is met: (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs; (b) the entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is created (e.g. building on the customer's land); (c) the performance does not create an asset with an alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date. Otherwise revenue is recognised at a point in time.
notes: (a) test: another entity would not need to substantially re-perform work done to date (ignore contractual/practical limits on transfer and assume no benefit of WIP). Payroll processing (SM Illustration 59) and a 20-day sea voyage (Illustration 60) meet (a).
No alternative use: assessed at inception on substantive contractual restrictions or practical limitations (significant economic loss to redirect). Interchangeable assets are not restricted.

Right to payment: at all times, amount at least compensating performance to date = costs plus a reasonable margin (a proportion of contract margin or the entity's normal margin), on termination for reasons other than the entity's failure. Meagre compensation for lost profit is not enough.
Audit opinion firm entitled to cost + 15% on termination → (c) met, over time (SM Illustration 61); customised satellite with payment right → over time (Illustration 62).
Equipment where the entity only keeps payments already made on termination (no right to cost + margin) → (c) not met, point in time (SM Illustration 63).
Payment due as work progresses but refundable if the customer terminates → no enforceable right to payment.
P.mem: Over time if: Consumed as you go, Customer controls the WIP, or No alternative use + Paid for work to date.

P.label: Ind AS 115.39–45, B14–B19
P.title: Measuring progress: output and input methods
P.law:
Use a single method per over-time performance obligation, applied consistently, to depict transfer of control. Output methods: surveys of performance, appraisals of results, milestones, time elapsed, units produced/delivered. Input methods: resources consumed, labour hours, costs incurred, time elapsed, machine hours. Remeasure progress each reporting date; changes are changes in accounting estimate (Ind AS 8).

Under a cost-based input method exclude costs that do not depict progress (wasted materials, inefficiencies). For goods not distinct, controlled by the customer well before the related services, significant to total cost and procured from a third party without significant design/manufacture by the entity, recognise revenue equal to their cost (zero margin) and exclude them from the measure of progress.
notes: Practical expedient (B16): if the right to consideration corresponds directly with the value of performance to date (e.g. a fixed amount per hour), recognise revenue at the amount the entity has a right to invoice.
Units-delivered output methods may misstate progress if WIP controlled by the customer is excluded.
Health club access → time-based straight line (SM Illustration 64). Stand-ready obligations → time-based if benefit is even or unpredictable.
Cost-to-cost with variable consideration: revenue = (fixed + variable) × cumulative cost ÷ total cost − revenue to date (SM Illustration 32).
P.mem: Uninstalled materials: take them out of the percentage, book them at cost.

P.label: Ind AS 115.38
P.title: Performance obligations satisfied at a point in time
P.law: If no over-time criterion is met, recognise revenue when the customer obtains control, considering indicators including: (a) the entity has a present right to payment; (b) the customer has legal title; (c) the entity has transferred physical possession; (d) the customer has the significant risks and rewards of ownership; (e) the customer has accepted the asset.
notes: Title kept only as protection against non-payment does not stop control passing.
Physical possession may not mean control: repurchase agreements and consignment.
Exclude risks that create a separate performance obligation (e.g. maintenance) when weighing risks and rewards.
Customer acceptance is a formality if the entity can objectively determine the product meets agreed specifications; otherwise control passes only on acceptance.
P.mem: Point-in-time indicators: P-L-P-R-A — Payment right, Legal title, Possession, Risks & rewards, Acceptance.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B64–B76
P.title: Repurchase agreements: forward, call and put options
P.law:
Forward or call option (entity's obligation or right to repurchase): the customer does not obtain control. Repurchase price < original selling price → lease (Ind AS 116) unless part of a sale and leaseback; price ≥ original selling price → financing arrangement: keep the asset, recognise a financial liability, and recognise the difference as interest (and holding costs). Compare prices considering the time value of money.

Put option (customer can require repurchase): if price < original price and the customer has a significant economic incentive to exercise → lease; if price ≥ original price and > expected market value → financing; if price ≥ original price but ≤ expected market value with no significant incentive, or price < original with no significant incentive → sale with a right of return. If an option lapses unexercised, derecognise the liability and recognise revenue.
notes: Sale and leaseback cases: keep the asset and recognise a financial liability under Ind AS 109.
Significant economic incentive: compare repurchase price with expected market value at repurchase and the time until expiry.
Sale ₹10 lakh with call at ₹11 lakh → financing: liability ₹10 lakh, ₹1 lakh finance cost over the term (SM Illustration 66).
Sale ₹10,00,000 with put at ₹9,00,000, market ₹7,50,000 → significant incentive → lease; ₹1,00,000 lease income over the period; if unexercised, revenue ₹9,00,000 at expiry (SM Illustration 67).
P.mem: Entity can buy back: below price = lease, at/above = finance. Customer can sell back: incentive decides.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B79–B82
P.title: Bill-and-hold arrangements
P.law: The entity bills the customer but keeps physical possession. Besides the general control indicators, all must be met for the customer to have control: (a) the reason is substantive (e.g. requested by the customer); (b) the product is identified separately as the customer's; (c) it is ready for physical transfer; and (d) the entity cannot use it or direct it to another customer. Consider whether custodial services are a separate performance obligation.
notes: Machine taken, spare parts stored at the customer's request, title passed, segregated and ready → revenue for machine and spares on 31 March 20X3; custodial service for 2–4 years recognised over time; transaction price split across three performance obligations (SM Illustration 68).
P.mem: Bill-and-hold: Substantive reason, Separately identified, Ready to ship, entity can't Redirect.

P.label: Ind AS 115.B52–B62
P.title: Licences of intellectual property: right to access vs right to use
P.law: A licence gives either a right to access the IP as it exists throughout the licence period (revenue over time) or a right to use the IP as it exists when granted (revenue at a point in time, when the customer can use and benefit from it). Right to access requires all three: (1) the contract requires, or the customer reasonably expects, the entity to undertake activities that significantly affect the IP; (2) the licence exposes the customer to the effects of those activities; (3) those activities do not transfer a good or service (are not a separate performance obligation).
notes: Licences include software, films, music, franchises, patents, trademarks and copyrights.

Character licence where the owner keeps producing and promoting the show → access, over time (SM Example 7). Team name and logo while the team keeps playing → access (SM Illustration 72(i)); dormant brand held by a brand collector → use (72(ii)).
1975 symphony recording, no obligation to change it, significant stand-alone functionality → right to use, point in time, even though paid monthly (SM Illustration 69).

Software with when-and-if-available upgrades: upgrades are distinct, so ignored in judging the licence → right to use (SM Illustration 70). Completed film with marketing that does not change it → right to use (Illustration 71).
Franchise with ongoing brand maintenance → access over time (SM Practice Question 4).
Sales/usage royalties follow the royalty exception.
P.mem: Access = the IP keeps changing because of you (over time). Use = the IP is static (point in time).

P.label: Ind AS 115.91–94
P.title: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract
P.law: Recognise as an asset the incremental costs of obtaining a contract (costs that would not have been incurred had the contract not been obtained, e.g. a sales commission) if the entity expects to recover them. Costs incurred regardless of whether the contract is obtained are expensed unless explicitly chargeable to the customer. Practical expedient: expense if the amortisation period would be one year or less.
notes: Test: would the cost arise if the parties walked away just before signing?
Capitalise: commission paid only on signing; bonus based solely on sales; sales manager's commission on contracts won by local staff (function or title of the employee does not matter).
Expense: travel to pitch a client; legal fees for drafting; salaries of sales staff.

1% commission on a ₹1 crore three-year contract: Ind AS 115 amortises over the three years; AS 9 expenses at once (SM Example 8 — the SM table states the amounts as ₹1 crore/₹33.33 lakh; check against the 1% commission before relying on the figures).
P.mem: Walk-away test: would you pay it if the deal died at the last minute? No → capitalise.

P.label: Ind AS 115.95–98
P.title: Costs to fulfil a contract
P.law: If fulfilment costs are within another Standard (Ind AS 2, 16, 38), apply it. Otherwise recognise an asset only if all: (a) costs relate directly to a contract or a specifically identifiable anticipated contract (direct labour, direct materials, directly related allocations such as supervision and depreciation of tools/right-of-use assets, costs chargeable to the customer, subcontractor payments); (b) they generate or enhance resources used to satisfy future performance obligations; (c) they are expected to be recovered.
notes: Expense as incurred: general and administrative costs not chargeable to the customer; wasted materials/labour not reflected in the price; costs of satisfied obligations; costs that cannot be distinguished between satisfied and remaining obligations.

Data-centre outsourcing: design ₹50,000 and migration/testing ₹1,10,000 under Ind AS 115 (amortise over 7 years including expected renewals); hardware ₹1,40,000 under Ind AS 16; software ₹1,00,000 under Ind AS 38 (SM Illustration 73).

P.label: Ind AS 115.99–104
P.title: Amortisation and impairment of contract cost assets
P.short: Amortisation and impairment of cost assets
P.law: Amortise on a systematic basis consistent with the pattern of transfer of the related goods or services (including anticipated renewals); update for significant changes as a change in estimate (Ind AS 8). Recognise an impairment loss to the extent the carrying amount exceeds the remaining consideration expected (ignoring the variable-consideration constraint, adjusting for credit risk) less costs still to be recognised. First impair assets under other Standards (Ind AS 2, 16, 38). Reversals are allowed, capped at the amortised amount without impairment.
notes: Five-year contract renewable yearly up to 10, average customer stays 7 → amortise over 7 years (SM Illustration 74).

P.label: Ind AS 115.105–109
P.title: Presentation: contract asset, contract liability, receivable
P.short: Contract asset vs liability vs receivable
P.law: Present a contract as a contract liability if the customer has paid (or payment is due) before the entity performs; as a contract asset if the entity has performed and its right to consideration is conditional on something other than the passage of time; and as a receivable if the right is unconditional (only time must pass). Receivables follow Ind AS 109; any difference on initial recognition between the receivable and revenue is presented as an expense. Excise duty included in revenue is presented separately (Indian addition).
notes: Interest from a significant financing component is shown separately from revenue.
Refund liabilities and right-to-recover assets are presented gross, not netted.
P.mem: Paid first → liability. Performed first: still conditional → contract asset; only time left → receivable.

P.label: Ind AS 115.110–129
P.title: Disclosures
P.law: Disclose: revenue from contracts with customers separately from other revenue and impairment losses on receivables/contract assets; disaggregation of revenue by nature, amount, timing and uncertainty (linked to Ind AS 108 segments); contract balances (opening/closing contract assets, liabilities, receivables; revenue from opening contract liabilities; significant changes); performance obligations (timing, payment terms, nature, returns/refunds, warranties); transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations; significant judgements (timing, methods, estimating variable consideration and the constraint, allocation); a reconciliation of revenue with the contracted price; assets from costs to obtain/fulfil (judgements, amortisation method, closing balances); and practical expedients used (para 63 financing, para 94 contract costs).
notes: The SM's listed-company extract (Hindustan Unilever, 2021–22) shows the accounting policy wording for revenue.

P.label: Ind AS 115 App. D
P.title: Service concession arrangements: features and the operator's rights
P.law: A private operator constructs or upgrades public-service infrastructure (roads, bridges, hospitals, airports, water, energy, telecom) and operates and maintains it for a specified period (build-operate-transfer etc.). Features: the grantor is a public-sector body (or a private body to which the responsibility is devolved); the operator manages the infrastructure and is not merely an agent; the contract sets initial prices and regulates revisions; the infrastructure is handed back at the end for little or no consideration. The infrastructure is not the operator's property, plant and equipment: the operator has access to operate it, not control of its use.
notes: The operator is a service provider: revenue for construction/upgrade services and for operation services under Ind AS 115; where both are in one contract, allocate by relative fair values.
Consideration for construction is recognised at fair value as a financial asset or an intangible asset.

Grantor-provided items the operator can keep or deal with are not government grants (Ind AS 20): recognise them at fair value with a liability for unfulfilled obligations. Infrastructure the grantor only gives access to is not recognised.

Disclosures: description, significant terms, nature and extent of rights and obligations (use, services, build, deliver at end, renewal/termination, overhauls), changes and classification; revenue and profit on exchanging construction for a financial or intangible asset.

P.label: App. D · FA vs IA
P.title: Financial asset model vs intangible asset model
P.law: Financial asset to the extent the operator has an unconditional contractual right to receive cash from (or at the direction of) the grantor — including where the grantor guarantees specified amounts or the shortfall between user receipts and specified amounts, even if contingent on quality/efficiency requirements. Measured under Ind AS 32/107/109 (amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL; interest by the effective interest method). Intangible asset to the extent it receives a right (licence) to charge users — not an unconditional right to cash because receipts depend on public usage; measured under Ind AS 38. If paid partly by each, account for each component separately at fair value.
notes: Borrowing costs: expensed as incurred unless the operator has a right to an intangible asset, in which case they are capitalised during construction.
Restoration/maintenance obligations (other than upgrades) are provisions under Ind AS 37 at the best estimate.

Toll road with ₹200 crore guaranteed by government → financial asset: Dr Financial asset 110 / Cr Construction revenue 110; construction cost 100 expensed; finance revenue 15; operation revenue 75 [(200 − 110) − 15]; cash 200 (₹ crore; SM Illustration 75(I)).
Expressway with toll collection from users → intangible asset: cost 110 expensed; Dr Intangible asset 200 / Cr Revenue 200; amortisation 200 over the operation period (SM Illustration 75(II)).
P.mem: Government guarantees cash → financial asset. You must collect tolls from the public → intangible asset.

P.label: Beyond SM · B44–B47
P.title: Beyond the SM: customers' unexercised rights (breakage)
P.short: Breakage on gift cards and points
P.law: Beyond the study material (Ind AS 115 Appendix B, paras B44–B47). A prepayment for future goods or services is a contract liability. If the entity expects to be entitled to a breakage amount (rights customers will not exercise), it recognises that amount as revenue in proportion to the pattern of rights exercised; if not, when the likelihood of exercise becomes remote. Amounts that must be remitted to another party (e.g. unclaimed property law) are a liability, not revenue.
notes: This is the mechanism behind 'only 80% of points will be redeemed' in the SM loyalty questions: unredeemed expected points are not deferred indefinitely; they are released as other points are redeemed.
Check the current standard text before quoting paragraph numbers in an answer; the SM itself does not discuss breakage separately.

P.label: Beyond SM · Ind AS 37
P.title: Beyond the SM: loss-making (onerous) customer contracts
P.short: Onerous contracts link to Ind AS 37
P.law: Beyond the study material. Ind AS 115 has no onerous-contract test of its own: a customer contract whose unavoidable costs exceed the economic benefits expected is assessed under Ind AS 37 (provision for the onerous contract), separately from the impairment test for contract cost assets under Ind AS 115.
notes: Fusion question risk: an Ind AS 115 contract plus an Ind AS 37 onerous provision in the same case scenario.
Contrast AS 7, which required expected construction losses to be expensed immediately.

Q.q:
New Way Ltd. decides to enter a new market that is currently experiencing economic difficulty and expects that in future the economy will improve. New Way Ltd. enters into an arrangement with a customer in the new region for networking products for promised consideration of ₹ 1,250,000. At contract inception, New Way Ltd. expects that it may not be able to collect the full amount from the customer.

Determine how New Way Ltd. will recognise this transaction?
Q.a:
Assuming the contract meets the other criteria covered within the scope of the model in

Ind AS 115, New Way Ltd. need to assess whether collect ion is probable.

In making this assessment, New Way Ltd. considers whether the customer has the ability and intent to pay the estimated transaction price, which may be an amount less than the contract price.

Q.q: A gymnasium enters into a contract with a new member to provide access to its gym for a 12-month period at ₹ 4,500 per month. The member can cancel his or her membership without penalty after three months. Specify the contract term.
Q.a: The enforceable rights and obligations of this contract are for three months, and therefore the contract term is three months.

Q.q:
Contractor P enters into a manufacturing contract to produce 10 0 specialised CCTV cameras for

Customer Q for a fixed price of ₹ 1,000 per sensor. C ustomer Q can cancel the contract without a penalty after receiving 10 CCTV cameras . Specify the contract units.
Q.a: P determines that because there is no substantive compensation amount payable by Q on termination of the contract – i.e. no termination penalty in the contract – it is akin to a contract to produce 10 CCTV cameras that gives C ustomer Q an option to purchase additional 9 0 CCTV cameras . Hence, contract is for 10 units.

Q.q:
Manufacturer of airplanes for the air force negotiates a contract to design and manufacture new fighter planes for a Kashmir air base. At the same meeting, the manufacturer enters into a separate contract to supply parts for existing planes at other bases.

Would these contracts be combined?
Q.a: Contracts were negotiated at the same time, but they appear to have separate commercial objectives. Manufacturing and supply contracts are not dependent on one another, and the planes and the parts are not a single performance obligation. Therefore, contracts for supply of fighter planes and supply of parts shall not be combined and instead, they shall be accounted separately.

Q.q:
Software Company S enters into a contract to license its customer relationship management software to Customer B. Three days later, in a separate contract, S agrees to provide consulting services to significantly customise the licensed software to function in B’s IT environment. B is unable to use the software until the customisation services are complete.

Would these contracts be combined?
Q.a: S determines that the two contracts should be combined because they were entered into at nearly the same time with the same customer, and the goods or services in the contracts are a single performance obligation.

Q.q:
Manufacturer M enters into a contract to manufacture and sell a cyber security system to Government -related Entity P . One week later, in a separate contract, M enters into a contract to sell the same system to Government- related Entity Q. Both entities are controlled by the same government. During the negotiations , M agrees to sell the systems at a deep discount if both P and Q purchase s the security system.

Should these contracts be combined or separately accounted?
Q.a: M concludes that the said two contracts should be combined because, among other things, P is a related party of Q , the contracts were entered into at nearly the same time and the contracts were negotiated as a single commercial package, which is clearly evident from the fact that discount is being offered if both the parties purchase the security system , thereby also making the consideration in one contract dependent on the other contract.

Q.q:
An entity promises to sell 120 products to a customer for ₹ 120,000 ( ₹ 1,000 per product). The products are transferred to the customer over a six -month period. The entity transfers control of each product at a point in time. After the entity has transferred control of 60 products to the customer, the contract is modified to require the delivery of an additional 30 products (a total of 150 identical products) to the customer at a price of ₹ 950 per product which is the standalone selling price for such additional products at the time of placing this additional order. The additional 30 products were not included in the initial contract.

It is assumed that additional products are contracted for a price that reflects the stand- alone selling price.

Determine the accounting for the modified contract?
Q.a:
When the contract is modified, the price of the contract modification for the additional 30 products is an additional ₹ 28,500 or ₹ 950 per product. The pricing for the additional products reflects the stand- alone selling price of the products at the time of the contract modification and the additional products are distinct from the original products.

Accordingly, the contract modification for the additional 30 products is, in effect, a new and separate contract for future products that does not affect the accounting for the existing contract and ₹ 950 per product for the 30 products in the new contract.

Q.q:
On 1st April, 20X1, KLC Ltd. enters into a contract with Mr. K to provide - A machine for ₹ 2.5 million - One year of maintenance services for ₹ 55,000 per month On 1 st October , 20X1, KLC Ltd. and Mr. K agree to modify the contract to reduce the amount of services from ₹ 55,000 per month to ₹ 45,000 per month.

Determine the effect of change in the contract?
Q.a:
The next six months of services are distinct from the services provided in the first six months before modification in contract, Therefore, KLC Ltd. will account for the contract modification as if it were a termination of the existing contract and the creation of a new contract.

The consideration allocated to remaining performance obligation is ₹ 270,000, which is the sum of

● The consideration promised by the customer (including amounts already received from the customer) that was included in the estimate of the transaction price and had not yet been recognized as revenue. This amount is zero.

● The consideration promised as part of the contract modification i.e. ₹ 270,000.

Q.q:
Growth Ltd . enters into an arrangement with a customer for infrastructure outsourcing deal.

Based on its experience, Growth Ltd. determines that customising the infrastructure will take approximately 200 hours in total to complete the project and charges ₹ 150 per hour.

After incurring 100 hours of time, Growth Ltd. and the customer agree to change an aspect of the project and increase the estimate of labour hours by 50 hours at the rate of ₹ 100 per hour.

Determine how contract modification will be accounted for as per Ind AS 115?
Q.a:
The remaining goods or services are not distinct, so the modification is accounted for on a cumulative catch-up basis:

ParticularsHoursRate (₹)Amount (₹)
Initial contract amount20015030,000
Modification in contract501005,000
Contract amount after modification250140*35,000
Revenue to be recognised10014014,000
Revenue already booked10015015,000
Adjustment in revenue(1,000)

*35,000 / 250 = 140

Q.q:
A construction services company enters into a contract with a customer to build a water purification plant. The company is responsible for all aspects of the plant including overall project management, engineering and design services, site preparation, physical construction of the plant, procurement of pumps and equipment for measuring and testing flow volumes and water quality, and the integration of all components.

Determine whether the company has a single or multiple performance obligations under the contract?
Q.a:
Determining whether a goods or service represents a performance obligation on its own or is required to be aggregated with other goods or services can have a significant impact on the timing of revenue recognition. In order to determine how many performance obligations are present in the contract, the company applies the guidance above. While the customer may be able to benefit from each promised good s or service on its own (or together with other readily available resources), they do not appear to be separately identifiable within the context of the contract. That is, the promised goods and services are subject to significant integration, and as a result will be treated as a single performance obligation.

This is consistent with a view that the customer is primarily interested in acquiring a single asset (a water purification plant) rather than a collection of related components and services.

Q.q:
An entity provides broadband services to its customers along with voice call service.

Customer buys modem from the entity. However, customer can also get the connection from the entity and modem from any other vendor. The installation activity requires limited effort and the cost involved is almost insignificant. It has various plans where it provides either broadband services or voice call services or both.

Are the performance obligations under the contract distinct?
Q.a:
Entity promises to customer to provide  Broadband Service  Voice Call services  Modem Entity’s promise to provide goods and services is distinct if  customer can benefit from the goods or service either on its own or together with other resources that are readily available to the customer, and  entity’s promise to transfer the goods or service to the customer is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract For broadband and voice call services -  Broadband and voice services are separately identifiable from other promises as company has various plans to provide the two services separately. These two services are not dependant or interrelated. Also the customer can benefit on its own from the services received.

For sale of modem -  Customer can either buy product from entity or third party. No significant customisation or modification is required for selling product.

Based on the evaluation we can say that there are three separate performance obligation: -  Broadband Service  Voice Call services  Modem

Q.q:
An entity enters into a contract to build a power plant for a customer. The entity will be responsible for the overall management of the project including services to be provided like engineering, site clearance, foundation, procurement, construction of the structure, piping and wiring, installation of equipment and finishing.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity have?
Q.a:
Based on the discussion above it needs to be determined that the promised goods and services are capable of being distinct as per the principles of Ind AS 115. That is, whether the customer can benefit from the goods and services either on their own or together with other readily available resources. This is evidenced by the fact that the entity, or competitors of the entity, regularly sells many of these goods and services separately to other customers. In addition, the customer could generate economic benefit from the individual goods and services by using, consuming, selling or holding those goods or services.

However, the goods and services are not distinct within the context of the contract. That is, the entity's promise to transfer individual goods and services in the contract are not separately identifiable from other promises in the contract. This is evidenced by the fact that the entity provides a significant service of putting together the various inputs or goods and services into the power plant or the output for which the customer has contracted.

Since both the criteria ha ve not met, the goods and services are not distinct. The entity accounts for all of the goods and services in the contract as a single performance obligation.

Q.q: Could the series requirement apply to hotel management services where day to day activities vary, involve employee management, procurement, accounting, etc?
Q.a:
The series guidance requires each distinct goods or service to be “substantially the same.” Management should evaluate this requirement based on the nature of its promise to customer.

For example, a promise to provide hotel management services for a specified contract term may meet the series criteria. This is because the entity is providing the same service of “hotel management” each period, even though some on underlying activities may vary each day. The underlying activities for e.g. reservation services, property maintenance services are activities to fulfil the hotel management service rather than separate promises. The distinct service within the series is each time increment of performing the service.

Q.q:
Entity A, a specialty construction firm, enters into a contract with Entity B to design and construct a multi-level shopping centre with a customer car parking facility located in sub- levels underneath the shopping centre. Entity B solicited bids from multiple firms on both phases of the project — design and construction.

The design and construction of the shopping centre and parking facility involves multiple goods and services from architectural consultation and engineering through procurement and installation of all the materials. Several of these goods and services could be considered separate performance obligations because Entity A frequently sells the services, such as architectural consulting and engineering services, as well as standalone construction services based on third party design, separately. Entity A may require to continually alter the design of the shopping centre and parking facility during construction as well as continually assess the propriety of the materials initially selected for the project.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity A have?
Q.a: Entity A analyses that it will be required to continually alter the design of the shopping centre and parking facility during construction as well as continually assess the propriety of the materials initially selected for the project. Therefore, the design and construction phases are highly dependent on one another (i.e., the two phases are highly interrelated). Entity A also determines that significant customisation and modification of the design and construction services is required in order to fulfil the performance obligation under the contract. As such, Entity A concludes that the design and construction services will be bundled and accounted for as one performance obligation.

Q.q:
An entity, a software developer, enters into a contract with a customer to transfer a software license, perform an installation service and provide unspecified software updates and technical support (online and telephone) for a two- year period. The entity sells the license, installation service and technical support separately. The installation service includes changing the web screen for each type of user (for example, marketing, inventory management and information technology). The installation service is routinely performed by other entities and does not significantly modify the software. The software remains functional without the updates and the technical support.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity have?
Q.a:
The entity assesses the goods and services promised to the customer to determine which goods and services are distinct. The entity observes that the software is delivered before the other goods and services and remains functional without the updates and the technical support. Thus, the entity concludes that the customer can benefit from each of the goods and services either on their own or together with the other goods and services that are readily available.

The entity also considers the factors of Ind AS 115 and determines that the promise to transfer each goods and service to the customer is separately identifiable from each of the other promises.

In particular, the entity observes that the installation service does not significantly modify or customise the software itself and, as such, the software and the installation service are separate outputs promised by the entity instead of inputs used to produce a combined output.

On the basis of this assessment, the entity identifies four performance obligations in the contract for the following goods or services:

• The software license

• An installation service

• Software updates

• Technical support

Q.q:
The promised goods and services are the same as in the above Illustration, except that the contract specifies that, as part of the installation service, the software is to be substantially customised to add significant new functionality to enable the software to interface with other customised software applications used by the customer. The customised installation service can be provided by other entities.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity have?
Q.a:
The entity assesses the goods and services promised to the customer to determine which goods and services are distinct. The entity observes that the terms of the contract result in a promise to provide a significant service of integrating the licensed software into the existing software system by performing a customised installation service as specified in the contract. In other words, the entity is using the license and the customised installation service as inputs to produce the combined output (i.e. a functional and integrated software system) specified in the contract. In addition, the software is significantly modified and customised by the service. Although the customised installation service can be provided by other entities, the entity determines that within the context of the contract, the promise to transfer the license is not separately identifiable from the customised installation service and, therefore, the criterion on the basis of the factors is not met. Thus, the software license and the customised installation service are not distinct.

The entity concludes that the software updates and technical support are distinct from the other promises in the contract. This is because the customer can benefit from the updates and technical support either on their own or together with the other goods and services that are readily available and because the promise to transfer the software updates and the technical support to the customer are separately identifiable from each of the other promises.

On the basis of this assessment, the entity identifies three performance obligations in the contract for the following goods or services:

a) customised installation service (that includes the software license);

b) software updates; and

c) technical support.

Q.q:
Telco T Ltd. enters into a two- year contract for internet services with Customer C. C also buys a modem and a router from T Ltd. and obtains title to the equipment. T Ltd. does not require customers to purchase its modems and routers and will provide internet services to customers using other equipment that is compatible with T Ltd.’s network. There is a secondary market in which modems and routers can be bought or sold for amounts greater than scrap value.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity T Ltd. have?
Q.a:
T Ltd. concludes that the modem and router are each distinct and that the arrangement includes three performance obligations (the modem, the router and the internet services) based on the following evaluation:

Criterion 1: Capable of being distinct

• C can benefit from the modem and router on their own because they can be resold for more than scrap value.

• C can benefit from the internet services in conjunction with readily available resources – i.e. either the modem and router are already delivered at the time of contract set- up, they could be bought from alternative retail vendors or the internet service could be used with different equipment.

Criterion 2: Distinct within the context of the contract

• T Ltd. does not provide a significant integration service.

• The modem, router and internet services do not modify or customise one another.

• C could benefit from the internet services using routers and modems that are not sold by T Ltd. Therefore, the modem, router and internet services are not highly dependent on or highly inter -related with each other.

Q.q:
V Ltd. grants Customer C a three- year licence for anti -virus software. Under the contract, V Ltd.

promises to provide C with when- and-if-available updates to that software during the licence period. The updates are critical to the continued use of the anti -virus software.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity have?
Q.a:
V Ltd. concludes that the licence and the updates are not distinct because the updates are critical to the continued use of the anti -virus during the licence period. C can benefit from the updates together with the licence transferred when the contract is signed.

Therefore, V Ltd. concludes that the licence and the updates are not separately identifiable because the software and the service are inputs into a combined item in the contract − i.e. the nature of V Ltd.’s promise is to provide continuous anti -virus protection for the term of the contract.

Therefore, V Ltd. accounts for the licence and the updates as a single performance obligation.

Q.q:
Media Company P Ltd. offers magazine subscriptions to customers. When customers subscribe, they receive a printed copy of the magazine each month and access to the magazine’s online content.

Determine how many performance obligations does the entity have?
Q.a:
